03 The read

Builds in public, failures included s1 s3

The site is not a portfolio, it is a dev log: versioned release posts that document what shipped and what went wrong. Combined with the public repos, the brand's core claim is receipts over résumé.

One identity, threaded end to end s1 s2 s4 s9 s10

The name, the domain, the GitHub handle, the npm scope, the LinkedIn slug and the X handle all interlink: site to GitHub, GitHub blog field back to site, npm packages back to the repos, and one handle carried across every platform. A stranger can verify the whole presence in three clicks, which is rarer than it sounds.

DevOps in print, AI agents in practice s5 s3 s1

The 2022 book fixes the public identity as a DevOps career author; the 2026 activity is almost entirely AI-agent tooling. The brand is mid-pivot, and the dev log is where the two eras visibly connect.

What is missing

  • The X account is now linked from the GitHub profile, but X still blocks logged-out reading — a stranger can find it and follow it, yet sees none of what it says.
  • The npm scope drops a letter (natjswenson, no 'e') — a searcher who finds the packages first can reasonably doubt they belong to the same person.
  • The LinkedIn profile blocks logged-out reading; it is findable only through the posts that carry its slug, so most of what lives there is invisible to exactly the stranger this report simulates.

A stranger searching this name meets several other Nate Swensons before the real one — a scientist, a principal, another software person — but the developer identity, once found, is unusually verifiable: site, GitHub, npm, LinkedIn and a published book all corroborate each other, one handle threading through every platform. The brand says: DevOps engineer who wrote the book on the career, now building AI-agent tooling in the open, documenting the failures on the way. The weak edge is reach — X and most of LinkedIn are findable but unreadable to a logged-out visitor — not substance.
